\[
Q = \min\!\left(255,\ \max\!\left(1,\ \left\lfloor \frac{Q_K\, s + 50}{100} \right\rfloor\right)\right),
\quad
s = \begin{cases} \lfloor 5000 / q \rfloor & q < 50 \\ 200 - 2q & q \ge 50 \end{cases},
\qquad
J(B) = \operatorname{IDCT}\!\left(Q \cdot \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{DCT}(B - 128)}{Q}\right)\right) + 128,
\qquad
\hat{I} = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{s} S_{-s}\, J\big(S_s I\big),
\qquad
q = 50
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(q\): The JPEG quality
- \(Q_K, Q\): The table of Annex K, and the table for quality q
- \(B\): An 8 x 8 block
- \(J\): The lossy step of JPEG on a block
- \(S_s\): A shift of the image by s, within the 8 x 8 grid
- \(n\): The number of shifts per axis

JPEG splits each plane into 8 x 8 blocks and takes the DCT of each block after subtracting 128. It rounds every coefficient to a multiple of its entry in a quantization table Q. Q_K is the table of ITU-T T.81 Annex K, scaled for the quality q as the IJG library does. The rounding makes each block jump at its edge. Nosratinia observed that compressing the decoded image again, with the same tables but on a shifted grid, smooths those jumps, since the new blocks straddle the old edges. Each shifted copy is a slightly different estimate of the original. Their average, over n by n shifts S_s, is smoother and closer to the original. With n = 1 and the original grid, the image comes back almost unchanged, since a decoded JPEG is already rounded on that grid.
